title: Demand-Driven Routing Space for Lattice-Surgery Compilation
authors: Hanyu Wang, Wan-Hsuan Lin, Zihan Chen, Eddy Z. Zhang, Jason Cong
abstract: Lattice-surgery compilation places logical qubits on a grid of surface-code tiles and routes their interactions. Sparse static layouts limit routing contention but reserve space that often remains idle. Reducing this reservation requires balancing area savings against additional gate serialization and qubit movement. In this paper, we present a co-designed dynamic architecture and compiler that allocates routing space according to circuit demand. The architecture preserves a fixed virtual qubit floorplan while allowing its physical spacing to change between execution stages. The compiler coordinates placement, scheduling, and routing to implement lattice surgeries using fewer physical qubits. Across our application benchmarks, our method reduces space-time volume by 55.6% in geometric mean and compiles 75.5 times faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration. A circuit-synthesis case study shows how our compiler exposes optimization tradeoffs.
summary: This work presents a novel, co-designed compiler and dynamic architecture for lattice-surgery compilation in fault-tolerant quantum computing. By allowing the physical routing space to adapt to the circuit's real-time demands, it significantly reduces the required space-time volume and dramatically accelerates compilation times compared to static methods. This advances the feasibility of implementing complex quantum algorithms on physical hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of minimizing the space-time volume required for compiling quantum circuits using lattice-surgery compilation techniques.
main_result: The proposed dynamic architecture and compiler reduce the space-time volume by 55.6% and compile circuits 75.5 times faster than existing static layout methods.
method: It introduces a co-designed compiler and architecture that dynamically allocates routing space based on the circuit's immediate demand, allowing physical qubit spacing to change between execution stages while maintaining a fixed virtual floorplan.
model_or_system: The system models quantum computation on a grid of surface-code tiles, where compilation involves routing interactions (lattice surgeries) between logical qubits.
key_observables: Space-Time Volume (Area * Steps), compilation speedup, and reduction in required physical qubits.
important_parameters: Circuit demand, virtual qubit floorplan, stage connectivity, and routing budgets ($\Delta H, \Delta W$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes a patch-layer abstraction and omits overhead costs like Clifford implementation or frame management.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate comparisons between static vs. dynamic layouts, showing space shifting between stages, and detail the compiler's workflow from floorplan initialization to step commitment.
paper_structure: The paper details the problem of static layout inefficiency, proposes the dynamic architecture, outlines the compiler's coordination of placement, scheduling, and routing, and validates the method against benchmarks.
why_interesting: While focused on superconducting/surface code architectures, the core concept of dynamically optimizing resource allocation (space vs. time) based on computational demand is highly relevant to resource-constrained quantum hardware design.
